## Trekking and ancient ruins: what to see in Ciudad Perdida, Colombia

The “Lost City” is an undisturbed pre-Inca settlement. It was discovered entirely by chance more than 30 years ago. For approximately five centuries, these ancient ruins lay almost buried near Colombia's Atlantic coast. Local tomb raiders stumbled upon the city in 1972. They found a trail of stone steps climbing a mountainside; following it led them to an abandoned city they nicknamed “green hell.”

When gold figurines and ceramic burial urns from the city began appearing in local markets, the authorities opened an investigation. In 1975, a six-day expedition led to the discovery of Ciudad Perdida (literally “Lost City”), also known as Buritaca-200. This archaeological site consists of the ruins of a Tayrona settlement in Colombia's Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta. The city is believed to have been founded around AD 800.

## Exploring Colombia's mountains

A trek to the Lost City (Ciudad Perdida) belongs near the top of the list for adventurous travelers and ecotourism enthusiasts. We set out with backpacks along narrow trails: there are no constructed roads or developed visitor facilities. It is precisely this remoteness that makes the area so appealing to lovers of challenging outdoor adventures.

## The Pearl Islands — Panama's own jewels!

The Archipiélago de las Perlas (Pearl Islands) consists of 90 beautiful islands. Their name comes from the large pearls once found in the surrounding waters.

## Pearl Islands — a place to unwind!

This is a wonderful destination for rest and relaxation, with white-sand beaches and clear, clean turquoise water. The archipelago's most popular island is Isla Contadora. This fifth-largest island was discovered by Balboa in 1514. Today it is one of Panama's leading holiday destinations, offering fishing, scuba diving, snorkeling and beautiful beaches. The island has plenty of restaurants, cafés, bars and nightclubs where visitors can enjoy an evening. The waters of the archipelago are home to large turtles, sharks and dolphins, as well as countless shoals of colorful tropical fish.

Zinacantán, also rendered as Sinacantán in some Russian-language texts, is associated with the culture of the Tzotzil people. The community is known for its textiles, embroidery and local artisans. Handmade objects offer a glimpse into traditions that residents continue to practice and use in everyday life.

A visit complements walks through San Cristóbal with an introduction to the highland communities of Chiapas. The focus here is on local patterns, colors and crafting techniques. Zinacantán is often combined with San Juan Chamula, where cultural life is expressed through religious customs. Together, the two places reveal the diversity of the region's traditions.

Zipaquirá draws travelers with the Salt Cathedral, Catedral de Sal. Its halls were created inside salt mines, so the architecture is closely bound to the underground rock. Visiting them reveals how a former industrial space became a religious and cultural landmark.

After exploring below ground, the visit continues in the town itself. A walk through Zipaquirá complements the cathedral experience with town streets, local establishments and souvenir shops above ground. The town is often visited on a trip from Bogotá, combined with Lake Guatavita and stories about the cultural history of this part of Colombia.

Brazil's Gold Route is a historic journey through Minas Gerais, shaped by the former centers of gold and gemstone mining. More important than any single road is the sequence of towns and places where the region's history can be read in its architecture, museums and mines.

Ouro Preto is the route's principal Baroque destination. From there, travelers can continue to Congonhas and Mariana, where old town centers and religious architecture sit alongside the heritage of gold mining. A visit to an old mine can be added in the Mariana area.

After the historic towns, travelers can spend a day at Inhotim, an open-air contemporary art museum. Belo Horizonte is then a convenient departure point for continuing a larger journey through Brazil by domestic flight. On the 14-day itinerary through Rio, Bahia and Iguaçu, this part of the trip falls between Rio de Janeiro and Salvador.
